title: Redwood & Acme HealthTech - Security & Privacy Review
summary: Acme HealthTech reviewed Redwood's SOC 2 posture, RBAC/SSO options, audit logging granularity, data residency, and encryption. Main focus was on how prompts and generated content are retained, handling of PII/PHI, and a formal confirmation that Redwood does not train on customer data. Redwood agreed to share SOC 2 Type II, architecture diagram, and KMS integration notes; next step is a POC/benchmark with stricter retention configs and a follow-up with legal and platform teams.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-19
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Martinez (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Rafael Gomez (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Acme CISO), Maya Patel (Legal), Sam Rivera (Platform), Dr. Nina Shah (Privacy)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro from our side, Alex here, I'll run the logistics. Priya and Rafael are our SEs who will dive into the tech bits. Jordan, do you want to kick off with what you want to cover?

[00:18] Jordan (Acme CISO): Yeah thanks Alex. Main items: SOC 2 / ISO evidence, how you manage RBAC and SSO, what the audit logs capture, and critically how you handle prompt retention and any chance customer data could be used for model training. We're a healthcare customer, so PII/PHI rules.

[00:35] Priya (Redwood SE): Totally understood. We'll go through each. At a high level Redwood is SOC 2 Type II in process - actually we completed the Type II as of Q2, we'll share the report. We support SAML-based SSO and SCIM for provisioning plus role-based access controls with granular roles for console and API.

[01:05] Maya (Legal): On the training question, can you provide a firm statement: do you use customer prompts or content to train public models or internal models? Must be contractual.

[01:20] Alex: Short answer: we do not train on customer data. We have a policy that customer data is not used to improve models. Priya, want to add where that's documented?

[01:30] Priya: Yeah, there's a section in our DPA and security docs - we will share a signed statement and the DPA language. For hosted API customers by default we retain request/response logs for 30 days for debugging and abuse detection, but you can opt out of retention and we have a private deployment that never persists prompts in the control plane.

[01:58] Jordan: That 30 days default - is that redactable? For PHI we need assured deletion.

[02:08] Rafael (Redwood SE): The default 30-day retention is configurable at the account level. For Dedicated and Private customers you can set retention to zero or enable local-only logging. We also offer a purge API that removes logs in bulk and a written attestation when purges are completed. The logs are encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys in our Dedicated and Private offerings.

[02:35] Sam (Platform): When you say customer-managed keys, is that KMS in the cloud or can we do an HSM? We have strict key rotation rules.

[02:44] Priya: We support both. For cloud-hosted instances we integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault. For Private deployments we can integrate with an HSM and you hold the root key. We'll share the KMS/HSM integration guide. Key rotation is supported and you can define rotation cadence; Redwood supports envelope encryption patterns.

[03:10] Jordan: Audit logs - what granularity? We need token-level tracing for requests associated with a user and ability to see who accessed what, when. Also want immutable logs for audits.

[03:25] Rafael: Audit logs include API keys used, user identity via SAML assertion or API token, request timestamps, model variant, and route. We capture metadata but not full prompt payloads in long-term audit indexes unless retention is enabled. For high-security customers we can log hashes of prompts plus per-request IDs and store the full payload only with consent. Immutable append-only storage is available and we support exporting logs to your SIEM (Splunk, Sumo Logic, or to S3).

[04:05] Dr. Nina (Privacy): You mentioned hashing prompts - is that reversible? If a regulator requests data, can you retrieve the original prompt?

[04:15] Priya: Hashing is one-way by design; we keep mappings only if retention is enabled. For PII / PHI access requests, if the customer requires full traceability we recommend the private deployment or Dedicated where you control retention and storage. For hosted customers we can run on-demand exports under legal process, but standard procedure is to follow the DPA and legal request flow.

[04:40] Maya: On the legal side we need explicit DPA language that states you don't train on customer data and that prompts will not be used for model improvements. Also need to confirm whether any telemetry or metadata could leak content.

[04:55] Alex: We'll provide the DPA excerpt and a short legal statement confirming no-training. There are a couple of telemetry fields (latency, model id, token counts) that are retained for billing and observability; those don't include prompt content. We do have optional diagnostics where a customer can opt-in to share example prompts - but that is explicit and requires consent.

[05:20] Jordan: Data residency - our data must stay in EU. Do you have region-restricted deployments?

[05:29] Priya: Yes. We have EU regions and can ensure data stays in-region for Hosted EU customers. For stricter controls we recommend Dedicated or Private VPC deployments in your region. Network egress controls and peering are available. We'll share architecture diagrams showing control plane versus data plane separation.

[05:50] Sam: For the POC, we want to simulate inference on PHI; what's your recommendation to avoid leakage?

[06:00] Rafael: Best path is Dedicated or Private deployment with customer-managed keys and retention set to zero. If Hosted is preferred, use tokenization/redaction on your side, and enable the "no retention" flag - we can also run the POC in an EU region. We'll provide a checklist for PII/PHI safe testing.

[06:20] Jordan: About RBAC - can we map SAML groups to roles and limit API key creation to admins only?

[06:29] Priya: Yes, SCIM provisioning maps groups to roles, and admin-only scopes can be enforced. Audit logs will show API key creations and rotations. We also offer short-lived credentials for automation to reduce long-lived secrets.

[06:45] Maya: Does Redwood support customer-managed tokenization or PII redaction within the service?

[06:52] Priya: We don't currently offer in-service tokenization that automatically redacts PII from prompt text. That's typically done on the customer side pre-ingest. However we do offer a plugins/hooks model for preprocessors in Private deployments where you can run redaction before data hits the runtime. We're evaluating native redaction features.

[07:15] Jordan: Regarding encryption in transit, are TLS certs mutual? How do you handle mTLS?

[07:22] Rafael: All control-plane and data-plane traffic is TLS 1.2+/1.3. We offer mTLS for Dedicated and Private deployments; for hosted customers mTLS can be added for peered networks. We'll share the network security spec.

[07:38] Alex: I want to address the model training question again since it's the top legal ask. Redwood's policy: we do not use customer prompts, conversations, embeddings, or any content tied to customer accounts to train our base or tuned models. That is documented in the DPA and our security FAQ. There are two exceptions: (1) explicit opt-in where a customer agrees to share data for benchmarking/training, and (2) aggregated telemetry signals used to improve system reliability (latency histograms, error rates) that do not contain content. We'll provide the legal phrase for contract inclusion.

[08:15] Maya: Good. We need that phrase exactly for our legal team. Also, for the exception 1, we need to see the opt-in flow recorded - how do customers opt-in?

[08:27] Alex: Opt-in is explicit via a separate agreement and opt-in flag in account settings; there is an audit trail for the opt-in event. We'll provide the flow diagram and the audit trail example.

[08:40] Jordan: On monitoring and alerts - if there's a suspected leak, what is the incident response SLA?

[08:48] Priya: Our incident response SLAs vary by contract tier; for enterprise/Dedicated customers we provide a 24-hour initial response SLO and a named incident manager. For hosted we triage within our security org and we will notify customers per the security notification policy. We will attach the incident response runbook excerpt.

[09:05] Sam: Do you have posture certifications beyond SOC2 - ISO 27001? HIPAA attestation?

[09:12] Alex: We have SOC 2 Type II and are in progress with ISO 27001 certification; we also provide HIPAA BAAs for qualifying customers and have a documented HIPAA controls matrix. We'll share current artifacts.

[09:26] Rafael: One more technical note: to reduce risk of accidental exposure via logs, we support prefix KV caching and partial response caching that can be disabled. There was a previous misreporting where someone called it KV cash in notes, I blame my accent - it's KV cache.

[09:45] Jordan: (laughs) Noted.

[09:55] Maya: A few legal clarifications: 1) confirm you will not resell customer data, 2) confirm no training on customer data, 3) data retention defaults and options, 4) access controls and who within Redwood can access customer data.

[10:12] Alex: 1) We do not resell customer data. 2) We'll provide a signed no-training statement. 3) Retention: default 30 days for Hosted, configurable to 0 for Dedicated/Private; purge API available and attestations provided. 4) Access is limited to authorized Redwood employees based on role; admin access is audited, and we have just-in-time privileged access (JIT) and session recording for sensitive ops. We'll include an access matrix.

[10:38] Dr. Nina: A practical question - if a user accidentally submits PHI in a prompt, what's the fastest way for us to get it purged?

[10:46] Priya: Use the purge API or file a support incident referencing the request ID; for enterprise we can expedite and provide attestation. If you're on Dedicated/Private and retention is zero, the data won't be persisted beyond processing. We'll include sample purge commands in the docs.

[11:05] Jordan: Are there any telemetry fields that could, even indirectly, reconstruct prompt content? For example tokenization artifacts that leak phrase structure?

[11:16] Rafael: That's a good question. Token counts and model selection metadata are not sufficient to reconstruct content. We avoid storing sub-token-level traces in long-term logs for Hosted customers. For debugging we can capture snippet examples but those are redacted and only visible to authorized personnel and by default stored for 30 days.

[11:40] Maya: Do you have an export pipeline to hand over all data in case of audits or subpoenas? How does that work with customer-managed keys?

[11:51] Priya: Yes, we support data export. For accounts using customer-managed keys we can export ciphertext that you can decrypt with your keys. For legal requests we follow the DPA and provide exports with a signed chain-of-custody.

[12:10] Alex: Quick note on contractual security add-ons: we offer extended retention controls, dedicated logging retention, and SOC 2/ISO evidence attestation as add-ons. Many enterprise customers take the Dedicated option and bind these in an SLA.

[12:30] Jordan: For the POC we'll likely need Dedicated or Private for our PHI sample. Can you give rough timelines to stand up a Dedicated cluster?

[12:38] Priya: Dedicated provisioning typically 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region; Private on-prem deployments vary more but we can scope. For the POC we can spin up a constrained Dedicated environment in EU within two weeks if capacity is available. We'll confirm capacity in the follow-up.

[12:58] Maya: On escrow and continuity - if Redwood goes under, how do we ensure our keys and logs are available?

[13:08] Alex: With customer-managed keys you own the root, so access to ciphertext requires your key. For logs we can set up cross-account S3 replication or a periodic export to your archive as part of the agreement. That will be in the contract addendum.

[13:26] Jordan: Any known incidents or breaches? We need a summary of recent security events if any and post-incident remediation details.

[13:34] Alex: We'll provide an incident history summary. No customer-impacting breaches in the last 24 months; we have routine vulnerability disclosures and patched them in our normal cycle. We'll include timelines and remediation notes.

[13:50] Sam: Regarding instrumentation, we want to ingest audit logs into our SIEM in near real-time - can you stream to an internal endpoint?

[13:59] Rafael: Yes, we can push logs via event streaming to Kafka or a forwarder, or export to S3. For high-volume export we recommend using our streaming connector with guaranteed delivery and backpressure. We'll share config examples.

[14:20] Maya: A contractual ask: include a clause that Redwood won't attempt to de-identify and then re-identify patient info ourselves - can you commit to that?

[14:29] Alex: Yes, we'll share proposed language. Our position: we don't perform re-identification attempts on customer data; we follow legal process for any investigative work.

[14:40] Jordan: For the POC, we will provide a small synthetic PHI-like dataset. We'll need instructions and a safety checklist.

[14:48] Priya: We'll deliver a POC checklist with redaction guidance, recommended retention configuration, and an isolated endpoint. Also sample terraform to provision dedicated capacity with KMS linked.

[15:05] Alex: Ok real quick recap of next steps: Alex to send SOC 2, DPA excerpt, and no-training legal phrase; Priya to send KMS/HSM guide and architecture; Rafael to send audit log schema and streaming config; Sam to send test dataset and we'll schedule POC start. Any additions?

[15:25] Maya: Please include the exact DPA clause and the opt-in flow for data sharing.

[15:30] Jordan: And confirmation of EU data residency for POC.

[15:34] Alex: We'll include all that. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with artifacts and schedule the POC kickoff.

[15:40] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mislabeling and small transcription errors, e.g., "KV cash" vs "KV cache", and speaker overlaps.
